extraction.rai:dataCollection: Multiple VQA datasets were created using different collection methods: DAQUAR used images from NYU-DepthV2 Dataset; COCO-QA derived QA pairs from COCO image captions using NLP algorithms; FM-IQA collected human-generated questions and answers originally in Chinese with English translations; Visual Genome used two distinct modes - free-form method where annotators asked any question, and region-specific method where workers were prompted to ask questions about specific image regions using descriptive bounding-box annotations; SHAPES consists of synthetically generated arrangements of shapes with systematically created questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include: NYU-DepthV2 Dataset images for DAQUAR; COCO image captions and images for COCO-QA; COCO images for FM-IQA; YFCC100M and COCO images for Visual Genome (108,249 images); synthetically generated shape arrangements for SHAPES dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For The VQA Dataset, annotators generated ten answers per question. For DAQUAR-consensus, an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is 83.3%. Inter-human agreement is especially poor for 'Why' questions, with over 59% of these questions having less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer. More than 13% of the 'yes/no' answers have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Ten answers per question for The VQA Dataset; average of five answers per question for DAQUAR-consensus
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: COCO-QA QA pairs are created using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions
extraction.rai:dataBiases: VQA datasets contain significant biases in question and answer distributions. Language bias is particularly problematic - question-only models can achieve 50% accuracy on COCO-QA without using images. Questions beginning with 'Is there' have 85.2% 'yes' answers. Binary questions in COCO-VQA are biased toward 'yes' answers (58% of the time). Annotators tend to ask questions biased toward 'yes' answers and include language 'clues' that systems exploit. Dataset bias significantly impairs algorithm evaluation, with easy questions (object presence, scene attributes) being overrepresented while harder questions (Why, Where) are rare.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Current VQA datasets are too small - training curves have not reached asymptotes. DAQUAR is particularly limited with only indoor scenes and significant clutter/lighting issues (humans achieve only 50.2% accuracy). Datasets lack sufficient variety in question types, with complex questions (Why, Where) being rare. Evaluation metrics have limitations - AccuracyVQA can be inflated (answering 'yes' to all yes/no questions yields 71% instead of expected 50%). Multiple-choice evaluation can be gamed by systems that learn to exploit answer biases rather than reasoning about images. Inter-annotator disagreement exists even for straightforward questions. Generic captions and descriptions are often ranked highly despite lacking specificity.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: VQA has significant potential social applications, particularly as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals to get information about images on the web and in the real world. It can improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content. VQA systems could enable image retrieval without metadata/tags. However, current systems' over-dependence on language bias and inability to properly reason about images limits real-world deployment and could provide unreliable assistance to users who depend on them.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: VQA datasets are used for training, testing, and validation of visual question answering systems. The datasets support multiple use cases including: training classification systems to answer questions about images, evaluating algorithm performance on various question types (object recognition, counting, spatial reasoning, common sense reasoning), benchmarking progress in combining vision and language understanding, and developing systems for real-world applications like assisting visually impaired users and enabling natural image retrieval.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Multiple VQA datasets have been publicly released since 2014, including DAQUAR (2014), COCO-QA, The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA), FM-IQA, Visual7W, and Visual Genome. DAQUAR has a variant called DAQUAR-consensus with additional ground truth answers collected. The VQA Dataset includes both COCO images and synthetic cartoon imagery (SYNTH-VQA). However, specific versioning policies, update timeframes, maintainer information, and deprecation policies are not detailed in the reviewed sections.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For Visual Genome dataset, two distinct modes of data collection were used: free-form method where annotators ask any question about an image, and region-specific method where workers are prompted to ask questions about specific image regions to combat bias in question types. For SYNTH-VQA, synthetic scenes were created using over 100 different objects, 30 different animal models, and 20 human cartoon models with deformable limbs and eight different facial expressions spanning different age, gender, and races to provide variation and reduce biases found in natural image datasets.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For image features, most algorithms use CNNs that are pre-trained on ImageNet, with common examples being VGGNet, ResNet, and GoogLeNet. For question features, various featurization methods are used including bag-of-words (BOW), long short term memory (LSTM) encoders, gated recurrent units (GRU), and skip-thought vectors.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: The most immediate is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. For example, as a blind user scrolls through their social media feed, a captioning system can describe the image and then the user could use VQA to query the image to get more insight about the scene. More generally, VQA could be used to improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content... Language bias in datasets critically affects the performance of the current VQA systems, which limits their deployment.

In the free-form method, annotators were free to ask any question about an image. However, when asking free-form questions, human annotators tend to ask similar questions about an image's holistic content... The creators of Visual Genome combated this by also prompting workers to ask questions about specific image regions... By using synthetic images, it becomes possible to create a more varied and balanced dataset. Natural image datasets tend to have more consistent context and biases... Using synthetic images, these biases can be reduced.
